hints: Identify the chiral carbon in $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$ by finding the carbon bonded to four different groups.
Recall how to show 3D arrangement with solid wedge, hashed wedge and straight bonds, and how the mirror image swaps two groups.
walkthrough:
Spot why alanine is chiral**
Look at the central $\text{CH}$ in $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$. It is attached to four completely different groups: $\text{-NH}_2$, $\text{-H}$, $\text{-CH}_3$ and $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. Any carbon with four different groups is a chiral centre, so two optical isomers exist.

Draw the first 3D tetrahedron**
Draw the chiral $\text{C}$ in the centre. Put two groups in the plane with ordinary lines, e.g. $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Then put $\text{NH}_2$ on a solid wedge coming out toward you and $\text{H}$ on a hashed wedge going back. This shows a true tetrahedron, not a flat cross.

Draw the mirror image**
For the second box, draw the exact mirror image. Keep $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ in the same in-plane positions but swap wedge and dash: $\text{NH}_2$ now on the dash and $\text{H}$ now on the wedge. Check the two cannot be superimposed by rotation, they are enantiomers.

Final answer: Two non-superimposable mirror images centred on the chiral $\text{CH}$ carbon bonded to $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. One isomer has e.g. $\text{NH}_2$ on wedge and $\text{H}$ on dash, the other has $\text{NH}_2$ on dash and $\text{H}$ on wedge, with $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ in the plane.

hints: Count the signals in the spectrum and remember that $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ protons exchange with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ and disappear.
Work out how many non-exchangeable proton environments alanine and glutamic acid each have in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$.
Use the n+1 rule to link the observed doublet near $\delta$ 1.5 and quartet near $\delta$ 3.8 to neighbouring protons.
walkthrough:
Remove the disappearing protons**
In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$, all $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ protons exchange to $\text{D}$ and give no signal. So for alanine, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$, you only see $\text{CH}$ (1H) and $\text{CH}_3$ (3H). That is two signals. For glutamic acid, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H)CO}_2\text{H}$, you only see $\text{CH}$ (1H) plus two different $\text{CH}_2$ groups (2H + 2H). That is three signals.

Match the number of peaks**
The spectrum shows only two groups of peaks, at about $\delta$ 1.5 and $\delta$ 3.8. That fits alanine exactly. Glutamic acid would need more than two, three peaks, so it cannot be glutamic acid.

Explain the doublet and quartet with n+1**
Splitting follows n+1, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbons. The $\text{CH}_3$ group is next to one $\text{CH}$ proton, so n = 1, giving 1+1 = 2, a doublet. The $\text{CH}$ proton is next to three equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ protons, so n = 3, giving 3+1 = 4, a quartet. This pattern is seen in the spectrum.

Contrast with what glutamic acid would give**
Glutamic acid has $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$ in its side chain. Each $\text{CH}_2$ is next to two protons, so you would expect triplets, further split by non-equivalence into multiplets. The absence of any triplet or multiplet confirms alanine.

Final answer: This is alanine in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$. Only two peaks are seen. Alanine has two non-exchangeable environments, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}$, whereas glutamic acid would show three environments. The doublet at $\delta$ ca. 1.5 is $\text{CH}_3$ split by one neighbouring proton on $\text{CH}$. The quartet at $\delta$ ca. 3.8 is $\text{CH}$ split by three neighbouring protons on $\text{CH}_3$. Glutamic acid would show two triplets or multiplets from $\text{CH}_2$ groups.

hints: Add the atomic masses for $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{NO}_4$ to find $M_r$, which equals $m/e$ of $M^+$.
walkthrough:
Add up to get the molecular ion**
Glutamic acid is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{NO}_4$. So $$M_r = (5 \times 12) + (9 \times 1) + 14 + (4 \times 16) = 60 + 9 + 14 + 64 = 147$$ The molecular ion $\text{M}^+$ therefore appears at $m/e = 147$.

hints: Compare 88 and 131 with 147 to find the mass lost in each fragmentation.
Recall common losses such as $\text{NH}_2$ (16) and side-chain cleavage, and keep the positive charge on the fragment.
walkthrough:
Use mass loss to identify the fragments**
Start from $M = 147$. For 131, the loss is $147 - 131 = 16$, which is $\text{NH}_2$. So the ion is the whole carbon skeleton without the amino group: $\text{}^{+}\text{CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H)CO}_2\text{H}$. Draw $\text{C}^+$ bonded to $\text{H}$, to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and to $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.

Assign the 88 fragment**
For 88, the mass retained is 88, formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{NO}_2^{+}$. This is cleavage of the side chain, leaving $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH-CH}_2\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ as a cation: $\text{[H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H)]}^{+}$. Draw $\text{H}_2\text{N}$ bonded to $\text{CH}$, which is bonded to $\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, with the + charge on N or C. Both representations showing correct connectivity and + charge are accepted.

Final answer: $m/e$ 88: $\text{[H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H)]}^{+}$, i.e. $\text{H}_2\overset{+}{\text{N}}=\text{CH(CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H})$ type fragment containing N and one $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group. $m/e$ 131: $\text{[CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H)CO}_2\text{H}]^{+}$, i.e. loss of $\text{NH}_2$ from the molecular ion.

hints: Think what type of solution resists pH change when small amounts of acid or alkali are produced at electrodes.
walkthrough:
Hold the pH constant**
Electrophoresis produces $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ at the electrodes, which would change pH and change the charge on the amino acids. So you impregnate the support with a buffer at pH 11. The buffer absorbs added acid or alkali and keeps pH, and hence ionic form, constant.
Final answer: Soak the paper or gel in a buffer solution of pH 11 / use a buffer to maintain pH 11.

hints: Recall the essential components: a support medium connected to a DC supply with positive and negative electrodes.
Consider where to place a negatively charged sample at the start so it can move a measurable distance toward the anode.
walkthrough:
Build the circuit**
Draw a strip labelled paper or gel soaked in buffer. Connect each end via buffer reservoirs to a DC power supply, with one end labelled anode (+) and the other cathode (-). The DC field is essential to pull ions toward oppositely charged electrodes.

Place the starting spot correctly**
Mark a small starting line with the mixture spotted in the middle of the strip, or slightly to the cathode (-) side. At pH 11 both amino acids are anions so they will move toward the anode (+). Starting in the middle or cathode side leaves space for them to separate as they migrate.

Final answer: Diagram shows a DC power supply connected to two electrodes with damp paper or gel strip between them, labelled anode (+) and cathode (-). Sample spot of alanine + glutamic acid mixture placed in the middle or towards the cathode side of the paper/gel.

hints: Use the given ionic forms at pH 11 to decide the sign of charge and which electrode attracts them.
walkthrough:
Follow the negative charge**
At pH 11 alanine is $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_3\text{)CO}_2^{-}$ (charge -1) and glutamic acid is $\text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2^{-}\text{)CO}_2^{-}$ (charge -2). Negative ions migrate to the positive electrode, so both move toward the anode (+).
Final answer: alanine: anode / positive electrode. glutamic acid: anode / positive electrode.

hints: Compare the charges of the two ions at pH 11 from the formulas given.
Compare their relative sizes or $M_r$ values and think how charge and size together control speed.
walkthrough:
Compare the driving force, charge**
At pH 11, alanine is singly charged (-1) because it has one $\text{CO}_2^{-}$ group, while glutamic acid is doubly charged (-2) because both carboxyl groups are deprotonated. Greater negative charge means stronger pull toward the positive anode.

Compare the drag, mass and size**
Alanine ($M_r$ ca. 89) is smaller and lighter than glutamic acid ($M_r$ 147), which alone would favour faster movement of alanine. However mobility depends on charge to mass ratio. The doubling of charge on glutamate outweighs its larger mass, so glutamic acid migrates further, leaving alanine behind over a shorter distance.

Final answer: Alanine has charge -1, glutamic acid has charge -2, so glutamic acid experiences greater electrical attraction to the anode. Alanine is lighter / has lower $M_r$ than glutamic acid, but charge effect dominates, so glutamic acid has higher charge to mass ratio and moves further (3.4 cm).
